conflicts.paper_a_claim: Yet, we argue that it is not sustainable to keep accumulating and maintaining all datasets for rapid access, considering the monetary and ecological cost of maintaining repositories.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: However, these costs are outweighed by the benefits of making research more reproducible, impactful, and equitable by facilitating the reuse of precious research resources by the scientific community.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Disagreement on the cost/benefit and sustainability of indefinitely keeping and curating all data for FAIR rapid access: one argues the monetary and ecological cost makes universal retention unsustainable (favouring cold archiving/disposal), the other argues the reproducibility and reuse benefits outweigh the costs of FAIRness.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Studies have shown that findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) data leads to improved data sharing in different scientific domains.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Sharing at both the project level and the journal article level was not carried out in the majority of cases, and when sharing was accomplished, the shared data were often of questionable usability due to access, documentation, and formatting issues.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether FAIR principles and data-sharing mandates translate into actual, usable data sharing in practice: a review-level claim that FAIR improves data sharing versus an empirical audit finding that mandated sharing largely did not occur and, when it did, produced low-quality/unusable data.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: We evaluated the content of the 358 DMSPs using the rubric developed for this study (Supplementary Material); 79.3% of them addressed all six required elements outlined in the NIH DMS Policy.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Of the 25 projects for which we attempted to locate shared datasets and generate a DATA score, nineteen (76%) had an overall score of 0 ( Fig 1 ).
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether data-management-plan mandates translate into realized data sharing: formal DMSP completeness is high (79.3% of NIH plans addressed all required elements), yet an audit of funded projects with data-management plans found 76% shared no locatable data at all (score 0). Plan completeness does not equate to realized sharing.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Meta-analyses showed a prevalence of declared and actual public data availability of 8% (95% confidence interval 5% to 11%) and 2% (1% to 3%), respectively, between 2016 and 2021.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: We identified 165 publications that reused OpenNeuro datasets
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether FAIR data sharing meaningfully happens in practice: a cross-specialty meta-analysis finds actual public data availability at only ~2% across medicine, whereas a purpose-built FAIR archive (OpenNeuro) documents substantial sharing and 165+ downstream reuse publications. Realized sharing/reuse depends heavily on dedicated FAIR infrastructure rather than default publishing practice.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Good data management is not a goal in itself, but rather is the key conduit leading to knowledge discovery and innovation, and to subsequent data and knowledge integration and reuse by the community after the data publication process.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: However, the Indigenous Data Sovereignty movement advocates for greater Indigenous control and oversight in order to share data on Indigenous Peoples' terms.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Governance orientation of data reuse: the FAIR principles frame maximal findability, accessibility and community reuse of data as the goal, whereas the CARE Principles / Indigenous Data Sovereignty insist that reuse be constrained by collective control, consent and benefit for the data's source communities. FAIR is data-centric and reuse-maximizing; CARE is people-centric and control-asserting - the two are presented as needing to operate together rather than FAIR alone.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Repositories must earn the trust of the communities they intend to serve and demonstrate that they are reliable and capable of appropriately managing the data they hold.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Even though hundreds of repositories are currently certified, we do not know if audit and certification of TDRs actually matters.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether formal repository certification demonstrably delivers trustworthiness/better preservation: the TRUST Principles paper assumes repositories should demonstrate reliability (implicitly via frameworks and certification), whereas the content-analysis study finds no evidence that audit and certification of trustworthy digital repositories actually improves preservation outcomes relative to non-certified counterparts.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Through systematic ontology mapping, we consolidated redundant, dispersed information into far fewer harmonized columns, reduced unique values, and increased the completeness of major attributes.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Specifically, FHIR-DS contained 1988 distinct DQ issues: nine ambiguous RD cases, two missing data items, and 1977 completeness issues induced by the FAIRification processes.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Opposite effect of metadata standardization/FAIRification on completeness: retrospective manual curation with ontology mapping increased metadata completeness, whereas an automated FAIRification (FHIR) transformation induced 1977 completeness issues relative to a direct export, i.e., degraded completeness. Dimension: whether standardization improves or degrades data completeness.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The concepts of the ISO/IEC 11179 metadata model automatically serve to make data adhere to FAIR data principles (), especially those addressing findability, interoperability, and reusability.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: For example, ISO/IEC 11,179 provides a general framework for metadata registries but lacks formal semantic relationships necessary for variable-level alignment across studies.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether the ISO/IEC 11179 metadata registry standard alone is sufficient for FAIR/semantic interoperability: one paper treats it as automatically conferring FAIR adherence, the other argues it lacks the formal semantic relationships needed for cross-study variable alignment and must be augmented with ontologies.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: authors publishing work in journals with mandatory data sharing policies were associated with nearly a tenfold increase in the odds of sharing data than those publishing in journals with no policy (OR: 9.5, 95% CI: 3.26–30.85).
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Even when authors indicate in their manuscript that they will share data upon request, the compliance rate is the same as for authors who do not provide the DAS, suggesting that the DAS may not be sufficient to ensure data sharing.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether journal data-sharing requirements translate into actual availability: a blanket mandatory-deposit policy is associated with ~10x higher odds of sharing, whereas a data-availability statement promising sharing on request yields the same (near-zero) compliance as no statement at all.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The result is an expanding family of ontologies designed to be interoperable and logically well formed and to incorporate accurate representations of biological reality.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Based on our analysis, we estimate that 64% of the UniProtKB proteins are incompletely annotated, and that inconsistent annotations affect 83% of the protein functions and at least 23% of the proteins.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Ontology developers assert coordinated ontologies deliver interoperable, accurate representations enabling data integration, but audits of the resulting Gene Ontology annotations find most protein annotations incomplete and inconsistent, undercutting the reliable-integration promise in practice.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The effectiveness of mandatory data sharing policies varied substantially by journal and type of data, a finding that might be informative for policy makers when designing policies and allocating resources to audit compliance.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Overall, we argue that universal open raw data mandates cannot adequately represent the diversity of qualitative research, and that MIRD may harm rigorous and ethical research practice within health psychology and beyond.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether open-data mandates should be universal: meta-research on (mostly quantitative) medical data treats mandates as effective levers worth strengthening and auditing, while a qualitative-research critique argues universal raw-data mandates are epistemologically and ethically inappropriate and can harm research quality.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The guidelines have been developed with input from a broad spectrum of stakeholders in the proteomics field to represent a true consensus view of the most important data types and metadata, required for a quantitative experiment to be analyzed critically or a data analysis pipeline to be reproduced.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: These shortcomings yielded large discrepancies in the analysis results (e.g., 13,068 vs. 4,923 proteins; 108 vs. 11 differentially expressed proteins), and, in one instance, a highlighted protein lacked robust support in the deposited identifications.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: MIAPE/HUPO-PSI reporting guidelines assert they capture the minimum metadata needed for a proteomics dataset to be critically re-analyzed or a pipeline reproduced, yet a 2026 reanalysis of six public PRIDE deposits found missing metadata and proprietary formats produced large reanalysis discrepancies - i.e. the standards are insufficient or unenforced in practice, leaving open-access data as non-reproducible 'data tombs'.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Only 11.5% of studies completely shared all phenotypes, while 37.9% shared less than 40% of the phenotypes.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: The impact of the shared data is evident in a growing number of published reuses, currently totalling more than 150 publications.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether depositing data in public repositories actually yields reuse: a systematic GEO audit finds most omics studies share badly incomplete metadata (only 11.5% fully), which limits secondary use, whereas a repository built on an enforced community standard (OpenNeuro/BIDS) documents substantial realized reuse (>150 publications) - suggesting enforced standards plus curation, not mere open deposition, drive reuse.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The findings indicate that while some groups are comfortable with metadata and are able to design a metadata structure that works effectively, many users are making little attempts to use it, thereby endangering their ability to recover data in the future.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Templates-based metadata is generated in parallel at each level enabling guided submission of experiment metadata.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Whether providing metadata infrastructure yields reusable metadata: the LabTrove ELN study finds free-form, user-defined metadata is largely under-used and threatens data recovery, whereas pISA-tree argues templated/guided ISA-model capture ensures standardized metadata. The disagreement is on whether tool design (free-form vs enforced templates) determines metadata quality.

conflicts.paper_a_claim: our results show that open data has significantly increased the citations of journal articles.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: We also find that sharing data in an online repository correlates with a smaller yet still positive citation advantage of 4.3% (±.8) on average.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Magnitude of the open-data citation advantage: a synthetic-control study of a Chinese economics journal mandate reports a large increase in article citations, whereas a 122,000-publication analysis finds only a modest 4.3% advantage for depositing data (and none for sharing code).

conflicts.paper_a_claim: Moral and altruistic motives encouraged engagement, whereas financial considerations played a minor, context-dependent role.
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Willingness to participate varied by incentive: 60.9% expressed willingness to participate when personal benefits were offered, 29.9% were motivated by public interest, and 9.3% declined participation altogether.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Relative weight of personal/material incentives versus altruism in driving willingness to share genomic/biomedical data: a systematic review concludes financial motives are minor and altruism dominates, whereas a national survey finds personal benefit is the single largest driver of willingness (60.9% vs 29.9% for public interest).

conflicts.paper_a_claim: The OHDSI distributed data network comprises over 331 data sources, containing more than 2.1 billion patient records across 34 countries [].
conflicts.paper_b_claim: Of the 75 concepts in the ELSO Maastricht Treaty, 19 (25%) were directly mappable to existing valid and standard concepts within the OMOP CDM.
conflicts.nature_of_conflict: Semantic adequacy/comprehensiveness of the OMOP common data model: a criteria-based review presents OMOP/OHDSI as the dominant, most-comprehensive CDM underpinning a 2.1-billion-record network, whereas a domain-specific evaluation finds OMOP vocabularies could represent only a quarter of core extracorporeal-life-support concepts without semantic loss, requiring a purpose-built extension.

papers.value_source_sentence: In contrast, 65 (21%) and 8 (3%) articles featured formalised, stand-alone sections dedicated to addressing data and code availability respectively (i.e. data and code availability statements).

figure_data.what_it_reveals: Data-sharing-statement prevalence varies three-fold across specialties/time (14% orthopaedics 2020-23; 21% oncology 2019; 42% gastroenterology 2018-23), reflecting uneven policy uptake; but even high-DSS fields show statements rarely correspond to obtainable data.

caveats: Oncology figure counts only formalised stand-alone DAS sections, whereas orthopaedics/gastroenterology count any DSS - oncology value is a conservative lower bound.
Different publication-year windows (2018-2023 vs 2019 vs 2020-2023).
All are top-tier/specialty journals, not field-representative random samples.

figure_data.comparison_name: How far deposited data fall short of reuse-readiness (metadata completeness / FAIRness / sharing rate)

papers.metric: % of important phenotypes (metadata) actually shared
papers.value_source_sentence: We observed that studies often omit over a quarter of important phenotypes, with an average of only 74.8% of them shared either in the text of publication or the corresponding repository.
papers.experimental_conditions: phenotype metadata presence in text or repository
papers.scope_population: human and non-human mammalian omics studies

papers.metric: FAIR-metric score achieved (of 25)
papers.value_source_sentence: The total scores achieved were 15.5 and 12 out of a maximum of 25.
papers.study_system: Dutch ICU databases on EHDEN portal (OMOP CDM)

papers.metric: % of full-text articles that link any dataset
papers.value_source_sentence: We found that 28.5% of 12 324 COVID-19 full-text articles in PubMed Central provided at least one dataset link.
papers.experimental_conditions: dataset URL link present in full text

figure_data.what_it_reveals: Across very different settings - omics metadata completeness (74.8%), OMOP-CDM FAIR maturity (15.5/25), and COVID-19 dataset linking (28.5%) - deposited data consistently fall well short of being fully reuse-ready, converging with the actual-availability audits on a persistent gap between deposition and usable reuse.

caveats: Metrics are not identical: phenotype-metadata completeness (%), FAIR-maturity score (of 25), and article-level dataset-linking rate (%) each measure a different facet of reuse-readiness.
Denominators differ (studies vs databases vs articles) and scales differ (percentage vs 0-25 score); a shared axis should normalise to '% of ideal'.
The EHDEN value is a small-n (2 databases) self-assessment, not a population estimate.

figure_data.comparison_name: Share of public records/requests meeting a metadata-completeness or reuse-fidelity bar

papers.metric: studies sharing all phenotypes
papers.value_source_sentence: Only 11.5% of studies completely shared all phenotypes, while 37.9% shared less than 40% of the phenotypes.

papers.metric: microarray entries reusable given standard formats
papers.value_source_sentence: Thus, we delve into the availability and processability of bacterial microarray data in GEO, showing a complex panorama where the lack of standard formats limits our reusability potential to at least 44% of the ~45 000 microarray entries.

papers.metric: request-publication pairs fully concordant on 3 characteristics
papers.value_source_sentence: Across four clinical data sharing platforms, data request proposals were often discordant with their corresponding publications, with only 25% concordant across all three key proposal characteristics reported by each platform.
papers.study_system: clinical-trial data-sharing platform requests (Vivli, CSDR, YODA, SOAR-BMS)
papers.experimental_conditions: concordance of proposed vs published analysis

figure_data.what_it_reveals: Across very different biomedical data-sharing settings, only a minority (11-44%) of public records or data-use requests meet full metadata-completeness or analysis-fidelity standards, illustrating a recurring reuse/quality gap.

caveats: Metrics are NOT the same construct: entry-1 is % of studies sharing ALL phenotypes (completeness), entry-2 is % of microarray records reusable given format standards, entry-3 is % of request-publication pairs concordant on analysis specification. n definitions differ (studies vs records vs request pairs). Use only as qualitative convergence that a minority of public records/requests meet a full-fidelity bar, not a like-for-like quantitative comparison.

figure_data.comparison_name: Quantified data-quality/fidelity gaps in real-world clinical data pipelines

papers.metric: source-EHR biomarker fields missing after FHIR export
papers.value_source_sentence: In contrast, biomarker data present in the source EHR were missing in 80%-100% of FHIR extracts.
papers.experimental_conditions: biomarker concordance: manual EHR review vs registry vs FHIR export
papers.method: retrospective concordance vs manual chart-review gold standard

papers.metric: vocabulary fields with substantial missingness
papers.value_source_sentence: The rule-based assessment identified substantial missingness in vocabulary fields (38/124, 30.6%) and missing or special characteristic values in relation to observations (3,643,581/15,313,287, 23.8%), measurements (25,583,622/642,623,715, 4%), care sites (28/1715, 1.6%), and deaths (117/34,330, 0.3%).

papers.metric: laboratory records with correctly assigned units before harmonization framework
papers.value_source_sentence: Before applying the framework, 73.1% (4,634,610,173/6,337,101,453) of records in the ConcertAI dataset had correctly assigned units based on the laboratory reasonable range table; after application, this increased to 99.7% (6,322,375,200/6,341,230,213).
papers.experimental_conditions: LOINC unit conformance before vs after framework

figure_data.what_it_reveals: Across independent real-world clinical datasets, standardization/exchange pipelines leave large, quantifiable gaps - from 80-100% biomarker loss on FHIR export, to ~30% missing vocabulary fields, to ~27% of lab records with nonconforming units before remediation - underscoring that adherence to interoperability standards does not by itself guarantee complete or faithful data.

caveats: Metrics are NOT directly comparable: ooag052 measures biomarker-field loss on FHIR export (n=30 patients), 68935 measures vocabulary-field missingness in an OMOP-mapped EHR (n=1.8M records), and 81254 measures laboratory unit conformance across ~6.3B records. Denominators and units differ (fields vs records); values are deficiency rates of different kinds and should be read as illustrative of a general phenomenon, not a like-for-like comparison.
